subject: mathematics
question_text: By using Cramer's rule, solve x − y + 3z = 5, 4x + 2y − z = 0, −x + 3y + z = 5.

mark_split.label: Write the system as AX = D
Find Δ = det A and check it is not zero
Apply Cramer's rule and state the solution

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.55, chapter 5 MATRICES, Long Answer question 9(v), Cramer's-rule route. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1+1+3 split gives one mark to each of the four determinants and three to the rule plus the stated solution, matching every other Cramer's-rule answer in this unit. ONE CARD PER METHOD: the book asks this one system by Cramer's rule, by matrix inversion and by the Gauss-Jordan method, and this bank answers each method on its own card so that a student who opens one never has to read another. The siblings are ts_ipe_m1a_mat_cramer_x_minus_y_3z_5_negx, ts_ipe_m1a_mat_inverse_x_minus_y_3z_5_negx and ts_ipe_m1a_mat_gauss_x_minus_y_3z_5_negx, and all three land on the same solution x = 0, y = 1, z = 2. A DIFFERENT system of a similar shape is already in the bank as ts_ipe_m1a_mat_cramer_x_minus_y_3z_5, whose third equation is x + 3y + z = 5 with a positive x; that card is not a duplicate of this one. PRINTED DEFECT IN THE STEM: the book prints the third equation as −x + 3y + 3z = 5, but every matrix it then writes uses the row (−1, 3, 1), that is −x + 3y + z = 5, and the book's own Δ = 50 and answer (0, 1, 2) belong to that version. This card is authored on −x + 3y + z = 5. The arithmetic settles it: with the printed 3z the determinant is 62, not 50, and the solution is x = 10/31, y = 5/31, z = 50/31 — fractions the book never prints; with z the determinant is 50 and the solution is (0, 1, 2), exactly what the book states. The book also mis-sets "x − y + 33 = 5" for x − y + 3z = 5 in its Cramer's-rule restatement of the same system. Both misprints are recorded here rather than silently repaired. Working checked twice: Δ was expanded along R₁ and again along C₁, both giving 50, and the solution was substituted back into all three original equations (5 = 5, 0 = 0, 5 = 5). Paper position: Maths-1A Section C prints 3 long answers at 8 marks each and the student answers any 2; Matrices is one of the units that can fill a Section-C slot. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by Cramer's rule — say what four determinants you need, how you build each one, how you get x, y and z, and how you check them.

steps.label: Write it as AX = D
steps.margin_note: First mark. A holds the coefficients in x, y, z order, X holds the unknowns, D holds the right-hand sides. Write the equations out in x, y, z order before building A — a missing term is the commonest error in the whole question.
steps.memory_tip: Line the equations up in x, y, z order first, so A holds the coefficients in the right places.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 3 \\ 4 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That the system is written as AX = D, with A the coefficient matrix, X the column of unknowns and D the column of constants.
accept: write the system as A X equals D where A is the coefficient matrix X is x y z and D is the constants
put it in matrix form with the coefficients in A the unknowns in X and the right hand sides in D
first write A X equals D taking the coefficients into A
modata AX equals D form lo rasta, A lo coefficients, D lo right side values
form the coefficient matrix the variable column and the constant column

steps.why: Cramer's rule is a recipe that reads off this matrix. Getting A right is the only place where the original equations are used, so every later step inherits any mistake made here.
common_mistakes: Writing the coefficients in the order they appear rather than in x, y, z order.
Missing a coefficient of 1 or −1 because the letter is written with no number in front.
Putting the constants into A instead of D.

steps.label: Find Δ
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Δ is the determinant of A itself, and it must be non-zero or Cramer's rule cannot be used at all — so say so in writing. Expand it a second time along a different row or column: a wrong Δ spoils all three answers at once and still looks like an answer.
steps.memory_tip: Expand Δ twice, along a row and then along a column. A wrong Δ spoils all three unknowns at once.

recall.must_convey: That Δ is the determinant of the coefficient matrix, that it works out to 50, and that being non-zero is what allows Cramer's rule to be used.
accept: delta is the determinant of A which comes to fifty and since it is not zero cramer's rule can be used
find the determinant of the coefficient matrix it is fifty which is not zero
expand det A twice to get fifty which is non zero so the method works
delta equals det A fifty, zero kaadu kabatti cramer rule use cheyyochu
the determinant of A is fifty and it must be non zero for this rule

steps.why: Cramer's rule divides by Δ. If Δ were zero the division would be impossible and the system would have either no solution or infinitely many — so the check is part of the method, not a formality.
common_mistakes: Computing Δ but never writing that it is non-zero.
Getting the sign pattern wrong when expanding: it is plus, minus, plus along the top row.
Using the constants column somewhere inside Δ.

steps.label: Find Δ₁
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Δ₁ is Δ with the FIRST column replaced by the constants 5, 0, 5. Columns 2 and 3 are untouched. Replace, never insert.
steps.memory_tip: Δ₁ REPLACES the first column with the constants. Columns 2 and 3 are untouched — replace, never insert.
lines: Replace C₁ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₁ is formed by replacing the first column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to 0.
accept: delta one is delta with the first column replaced by the constants and it comes to zero
put the constants into the first column and expand to get zero
replace column one with the right hand side values giving delta one equal to zero
first column place lo constants pettithe delta one zero vasthundi
swap the first column for the constant column and the determinant is zero

steps.why: Δ₁ pairs with x because x is the first unknown. The subscript is a position, not a name — which is why the constants go into column one and nowhere else.
common_mistakes: Replacing a row instead of a column.
Replacing the second column and later dividing it into x.
Adding a fourth column instead of replacing one.

steps.label: Find Δ₂
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Same move, second column. Column 1 goes back to the coefficients of x — a common slip is to leave the constants there from the previous step.
steps.memory_tip: Second column now, and column 1 goes BACK to the x coefficients. Leaving the constants there is the usual slip.
lines: Replace C₂ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₂ is formed by replacing the second column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to 50.
accept: delta two is delta with the second column replaced by the constants and it equals fifty
put the constants into the middle column and expand to get fifty
replace column two with the constant column giving fifty
second column lo constants pettithe delta two fifty vasthundi
the middle column becomes the constants and the determinant is fifty

steps.why: Each unknown gets the determinant whose replaced column is that unknown's own column in A. y sits in column two, so Δ₂ is y's determinant.
common_mistakes: Leaving the constants in column one from the previous step, so two columns are wrong at once.
Forgetting the minus in front of the middle term when expanding along the top row.

steps.label: Find Δ₃
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Last one — third column replaced, the other two back to the coefficients.
steps.memory_tip: Third column replaced, the other two back to the coefficients.
lines: Replace C₃ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₃ is formed by replacing the third column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to 100.
accept: delta three is delta with the third column replaced by the constants and it comes to one hundred
put the constants into the last column and expand to get one hundred
replace column three with the constant column giving one hundred
third column lo constants pettithe delta three one hundred vasthundi
the last column becomes the constants and the determinant is one hundred

steps.why: Three unknowns need three replaced determinants, plus Δ itself. Four determinants is always the cost of Cramer's rule on a 3×3 system, and knowing that in advance is how you budget the time.
common_mistakes: Stopping after Δ₂ and trying to find z by substitution.
Leaving an earlier replacement in place.

steps.label: Apply Cramer's rule
steps.margin_note: The last three marks. Δ₁ comes out 0, so x = 0. A zero on TOP is a perfectly good answer; only Δ itself is forbidden to be zero. Put all three values back into the three original equations before stopping.
steps.memory_tip: Each unknown is its own determinant over Δ. Then put the three values back into all three original equations before you stop.
lines: Substitute back into the three equations:

recall.must_convey: That each unknown is its own determinant divided by Δ, giving x = 0, y = 1, z = 2, and that the values are checked in all three original equations.
accept: x is delta one by delta y is delta two by delta and z is delta three by delta giving x equals zero y equals one z equals two
divide each of the three determinants by delta to get x equals zero y equals one z equals two
by cramer's rule each unknown is its own determinant over delta so the solution is x equals zero y equals one z equals two
prathi determinant ni delta tho divide cheste x equals zero y equals one z equals two vasthundi
delta one over delta gives x and similarly y and z then substitute back to check
reject: x equals zero y equals one z equals two

steps.why: The whole method exists so that each unknown can be found on its own, without eliminating anything. Substituting back is the only check that catches a slip inside Δ₁, Δ₂ or Δ₃, because an error there spoils one unknown and leaves the other two looking right.
common_mistakes: Dividing Δ by Δ₁ instead of Δ₁ by Δ.
Calling x = 0/50 undefined; a zero on top gives x = 0.
Stopping without substituting the three values back into all three equations.
